title: Delirious
full_review:
The aptly titled "Delirious" (Peace Arch/Thema/Artina) tells the story of an unlikely friendship that is put to the test, and nearly destroyed by an even more unlikely romance. The film combines the crisp pacing of a music video with the outsized emotions of grand opera. But its attempt to move between grim realism and unabashed optimism leads, in the end, to an unconvincing muddle.

At the heart of the story is the figure of Toby Grace (Michael Pitt), a young homeless man whose gentle manner has a winning effect on just about everyone he meets. This includes the film's other main protagonist, Les Galantine (Steve Buscemi), a crude and seemingly ruthless "paparazzo" who nonetheless takes in Toby and gradually becomes both his friend and mentor.

Les makes his living by preying on the vulnerabilities of the famous, and -- for a while at least -- Toby, as his "assistant," is happy to do the same. Conflicts between the two arise, however, as soon as Toby himself begins to cross the line from obscurity to celebrity.

His first step in this direction comes when he has the opportunity to meet pop-music diva K'Harma Leeds (Alison Lohman), a young woman he has long worshipped from afar. Happily for Toby, she turns out to be just as susceptible to his charm as everyone else seems to be, and a romance between the two is quickly ignited.

This situation presents a dilemma for Les, who, despite his insistence that the rich and famous are just the same as everyone else, cannot handle the transition from outsider to insider, from parasite to pal.

There are some impressive performances here. No one, after all, can do more with the part of a lovable lowlife than Buscemi, while Pitt manages to make the Candide-like Toby appear genuinely innocent, as opposed to merely obtuse.

The script also has its strengths, particularly the wit with which it dissects some of the mores of the contemporary entertainment industry. But the tone of the film veers disconcertingly from bleak cynicism to an almost sophomoric indulgence in fantasy. Toby's sudden ascent from homelessness to fame is as inexplicable as later plot developments involving Les.

The values that writer-director Tom DiCillo's film upholds are also problematic at times. Les' parents, for instance, are presented as uncaring and even cruel because they refuse to affirm the value of his work. Since the example of his work in question is an incredibly humiliating photograph of a celebrity in a vulnerable situation, however, the more pertinent question may be why his parents have failed to instill in Les even the most basic sense of human empathy. Equally troubling is the fact that Toby, who is consistently presented in a positive light, thinks nothing of romancing another woman strictly for career advancement.

The film contains relentless rough and crude language and some profanity, much crude humor, rear and partial nudity, some skimpy costuming, innuendo and implied unmarried sexual liaisons. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. Not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America.
